Podcasts / Interviews.raw_text: We can really now start guiding the experimentation. So where before you, we built these human cell atlases, we had sort of this mapping aspect. Then we talked about the world models prediction problem. From mapping, we went to prediction. But now we can go to actually steering the next experiment. But quite frankly, very often the papers ended with some model, right? Maybe some sort of concept figure, maybe add a little bit validation. But then typically you start the next project, right? And of course you learn a bit, but it's not like, not like a continual learning type of thing. A new thing we ca-- which we call Lab Compass, which is an inverse generative model that actually allows you, once you have a forward world model or whatever, to tell you what you need to do in order to reach a certain state. Obviously, the, the ultimate vision being that we want to RL everything. We want to do RL also in, in this loop. It it's a bit out there, but you know, I think we're s- we're slowly getting there. Welcome to the Latent Space AI for Science podcast. I'm RJ Hanocki, CTO of Mira Omics. I'm joined by my co-host, Brandon Anderson, who develops RNA therapeutics at Atomic AI. I can't emphasize enough how much Fabian Theis and his labs and companies have contributed to the development of systems biology and various iterations of the virtual cell concept. Papers and models come out of his lab faster than I can read them, and the lab is consistently moving the ball forward on our understanding of how to observe and model the behaviors and the interactions of cells. Just as importantly, his work often focuses on creating the tools that researchers and scientists actually use in their day-to-day work. Most computational biologists have probably used Scanpy and Anndata at some point, and this work has led to the creation of scVerse, which is an amazing collection of open tools that has attracted many, many contributors. Of course, Fabian is one of those academics who has way more honors than you can possibly list, but suffice it to say that he leads a bunch of the AI and computational biology efforts at Helmholtz Munich and related institutions, and participates also in many other industry efforts. Fabian, it's really great to meet you. Thanks a lot for joining us. Thanks for having me. I'm really looking forward to the discussion, man. Yeah, I've been tracking your work for a long time, and so it's a great honor to finally get you on the show and talk to you. Let's kick things off with some of the hype happening right now. There's a ton of interest right now in structural biology. Anthropic and OpenAI biopharma initiatives focus heavily on designing molecules right now. On the other hand, virtual cell and systems biology approaches really haven't gotten as much attention recently. Maybe Zera and Noetic are good counter examples there. events.raw_text: We can really now start guiding the experimentation. So where before you, we built these human cell atlases, we had sort of this mapping aspect. Then we talked about the world models prediction problem. From mapping, we went to prediction. But now we can go to actually steering the next experiment. But quite frankly, very often the papers ended with some model, right? Maybe some sort of concept figure, maybe add a little bit validation. But then typically you start the next project, right? And of course you learn a bit, but it's not like, not like a continual learning type of thing. A new thing we ca-- which we call Lab Compass, which is an inverse generative model that actually allows you, once you have a forward world model or whatever, to tell you what you need to do in order to reach a certain state. Obviously, the, the ultimate vision being that we want to RL everything. We want to do RL also in, in this loop. It it's a bit out there, but you know, I think we're s- we're slowly getting there. Welcome to the Latent Space AI for Science podcast. I'm RJ Hanocki, CTO of Mira Omics. I'm joined by my co-host, Brandon Anderson, who develops RNA therapeutics at Atomic AI. I can't emphasize enough how much Fabian Theis and his labs and companies have contributed to the development of systems biology and various iterations of the virtual cell concept. Papers and models come out of his lab faster than I can read them, and the lab is consistently moving the ball forward on our understanding of how to observe and model the behaviors and the interactions of cells. Just as importantly, his work often focuses on creating the tools that researchers and scientists actually use in their day-to-day work. Most computational biologists have probably used Scanpy and Anndata at some point, and this work has led to the creation of scVerse, which is an amazing collection of open tools that has attracted many, many contributors. Of course, Fabian is one of those academics who has way more honors than you can possibly list, but suffice it to say that he leads a bunch of the AI and computational biology efforts at Helmholtz Munich and related institutions, and participates also in many other industry efforts. Fabian, it's really great to meet you. Thanks a lot for joining us. Thanks for having me. I'm really looking forward to the discussion, man. Yeah, I've been tracking your work for a long time, and so it's a great honor to finally get you on the show and talk to you. Let's kick things off with some of the hype happening right now. There's a ton of interest right now in structural biology. Anthropic and OpenAI biopharma initiatives focus heavily on designing molecules right now. On the other hand, virtual cell and systems biology approaches really haven't gotten as much attention recently. Maybe Zera and Noetic are good counter examples there.
